subject: Re: Helios Health — capacity & quantization plan for Dedicated pool

Subject: Helios POC — sizing inputs and preferred quantization

Hi Laura / Marcus,

Thanks again for yesterday's demo — it was really helpful. We're moving the Helios POC forward and procurement asked for a concrete sizing recommendation for Dedicated capacity that maps to our workloads. A few specifics from our side:

- Production peak: ~70 r/s sustained at 95th percentile for short chat flows; spikes to ~200 r/s for batched inference windows during reporting loads.
- Prominent model variants: a tuned Llama-3-70B-32k used for clinical summarization (32k context) and a lighter 13B chat model for front-end interactions (8k context).
- We plan to enable CPU offload during overnight batch runs if it's cost-effective.
- Preference is aggressive int8 quantization if model quality checks pass; procurement asked for risk notes versus fp16.

Can you share: (a) expected GPU footprint per model variant with and without KV cache offload, (b) impact on concurrency when switching to int8/4-bit, and (c) a suggested dedicated pool topology we can reference in the SOW.

Attaching our PoC spec (small). happy to jump on a call if helpful.

Best,
Sophie Turner
Head of ML Ops, Helios Health

Attachment: helios_poc_spec.pdf (1.2MB)

Hi Sophie — thanks for the clear inputs and the spec. Looping Marcus and Connor for the engineering sizing and operational plan. High level answers up front:

- We'll provide per-variant GPU memory footprints for 8k and 32k contexts, with three execution profiles: fp16 (baseline), int8 (recommended for cost), and mixed int4 fallback (experimental).
- KV-cache behavior is the dominant driver for the 32k summarization model. We'll show two modes: in-GPU KV (lowest latency, highest RAM) and host-offload (lower capacity needs, ~15-30ms added tail latency per request depending on cache-hit patterns).
- Suggested Dedicated pool: a two-tier pool with a high-memory, low-latency lane for 32k summarization (NVIDIA H100-style instances with 80–128GB GPU RAM equivalents) and a standard lane for 8k chat (A100/RTX-class or quantized variants). Autoscale windows tuned to diurnal usage and a burst buffer for reporting spikes.

Marcus will drop detailed numbers and a simple capacity table; Connor will add rollout/canary guidance and monitoring hooks we recommend for the SOW. Expect a single document from us in ~3 business days.

Thanks —
Laura Bennett
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Helios POC — sizing inputs and preferred quantization

Sophie / Laura — digging into the numbers. I ran memory-modeling against the Helios spec and produced conservative and optimistic footprints; summary below (attached full modeling workbook). These are per-instance footprints (not total pool sizing):

1) 13B chat model (8k context)
- fp16 baseline: ~32GB GPU memory (model + kv cache average for 2k median length), supports ~8 concurrent steady r/s per 80GB GPU-equivalent when batching at 8–16 tokens/batch.
- int8 (dynamic quant): memory delta ~ -25% => ~24GB; concurrency improves ~1.5x due to smaller activation memory and improved kernel throughput.
- int4 (experimental): further -10–12% memory, but we observed token rate variance and occasional decode stalls in our perf tests — risk parameter small but non-zero.

2) 70B summarization model (32k context) — KV is the killer here
- fp16 w/in-GPU KV: worst-case ~110–130GB GPU memory to hold long-context KV + model activations. This requires large-memory instances or multi-GPU sharding.
- fp16 with host-offload (streaming KV pages to host RAM + async prefetch): reduces GPU resident memory to ~48–64GB but adds tail latency ~12–35ms depending on hit locality.
- int8 with host-offload: GPU resident down to ~36–48GB; with careful calibration of prefix caching we maintain 95p latency targets for chat-like flows.
- int8 in-GPU (no offload): still ~85–100GB — better latency, higher cost.

Operational recommendations and trade-offs:
- If Helios needs sub-50ms p95 for 32k summarization, target in-GPU KV with 2x high-memory GPUs behind a routing policy that prioritizes the summarization lane.
- If 80–120ms p95 is acceptable, prefer host-offload + int8: ~55% reduction in GPU capacity needs and substantial monthly cost savings.
- For overnight batch reports where throughput matters and latency can be relaxed, we recommend a cheap CPU-offload path (persistent KV pages on host SSD + offline batching) — this reduces peak GPU count by ~30% for those windows.

Suggested Dedicated pool topology (initial commit):
- 4x high-memory GPU instances (80–128GB-equivalent) reserved for 32k summarization (can be mixed precision/int8).
- 6x standard GPU instances (40–48GB-equivalent) for chat and burst handling.
- 2x autoscale spare slots for ephemeral bursts (pre-warm policy at 180s).
- Global buffer of host memory nodes for KV-offload and prefetching; ensure network NICs are capable of 100Gbps to avoid offload tail latency spikes.

Sizing math note (conservative): assume 20% cache miss amplification (prefetch misses) for first 6 weeks of PoC; re-evaluate after telemetry.

I've attached the kv_memory_modeling.xlsx and a small CSV of offload_profiles we used for latency simulations. Connor — see below for rollout hooks and canary thresholds I used; we should include them in the SOW.

Best,
Marcus Lin
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachments: kv_memory_modeling.xlsx, offload_profiles_v2.csv

Thanks team — quick operational addendum and SOW bullets for procurement. Quoting the important pieces so procurement has explicit SLAs and rollback behavior:

- Canary rollout: route 5% of 32k traffic to host-offload/int8 lane for 48 hours, observe 95p latency and failure rate (target: 95p <= 120ms, error rate < 0.5%).
- Fallback policy: automatic routing back to in-GPU lane if 95p latency > 150ms or error rate spikes > 1% for 5 consecutive minutes.
- Monitoring: token-level cost, KV cache hit ratio, per-request KV page fetch time, and GPU memory pressure. We will surface these in a per-route Redwood Console dashboard.
- Procurement SOW wording: "Reserved pool: 4 high-memory GPU nodes + 6 standard nodes. Redwood will provide telemetry and 30-day performance tuning period. Customer may request an SLA credit if average 95p latency for critical summarization routes exceeds 150ms over a rolling 7-day window."

Sophie — if you confirm the SLA phrasing and the initial pool counts, Jordan and I will draft the SOW appendix and associated procurement numbers (monthly committed GPU hours, estimated monthly token cost).

Connor O'Brien
Principal Customer Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference
